title: Pareus: in this life the freed will can still do good and evil
source_text: XLII. Neque sic in hac vita per gratiam liberatur hominis arbitrium, quin semper, ut bene, sic male agere possit: sicut ultro Paraeus contra Bellarminum disputans agnoscit. Quis Christianus, inquit, unquam dubitavit hominem donatum gratia arbitrium habere liberatum & liberum ad bonum eligendum, praestandum ex vi gratiae: ad malum quoque eligendum, faciendum ex imbecillitate naturae, quae a gratia nec regeneratur, nec regitur perfecte in hac vita: unde renati libertate voluntatis, tam ad bene quam ad male operandum, in hac vita utuntur? Nulla igitur haec quaestio esse potest, utrum posito gratiae auxilio homo sit vere liberi arbitrii? In librum V. Bellarmini de Gratia & libero arbitrio, capite XIII. Quibus conformia sunt quae repetit author ille, ejusdem libri capite XXVIII. In statu gratiae sic libere eligit bonum voluntas renovata, ut dum ad id eligendum efficaciter movetur a gratia, possit quidem contrarium eligere per defectum naturae, nolit vero per efficaciam gratiae.
pass_a_gloss: XLII. Nor is the choice of man so freed in this life through grace, that it can not always, as well, so badly act: as Pareus disputing against Bellarmine of his own accord acknowledges. What Christian, he says, ever doubted that man endowed with grace has choice freed and free for choosing good, performing it from the force of grace: for choosing evil also, doing it from the weakness of nature, which by grace is neither regenerated, nor ruled perfectly in this life: whence the reborn use liberty of will, both for working well and for working badly, in this life? There can therefore be no question this, whether with the help of grace posited man be truly of free choice? On book V of Bellarmine on Grace and free choice, chapter XIII. With which agree the things which that author repeats, in chapter XXVIII of the same book. In the state of grace the renewed will so freely chooses good, that while to choose it it is efficaciously moved by grace, it can indeed choose the contrary through the defect of nature, but will not through the efficacy of grace.
pass_b_english: Thesis XLII. Nor is man's choice so freed by grace in this life that he cannot always act badly as well as well, as Pareus, disputing against Bellarmine, freely admits. 'What Christian,' he says, 'ever doubted that a man endowed with grace has a choice that is set free and free to choose good and do it by the power of grace, and also to choose evil and do it out of the weakness of nature, which grace neither regenerates nor governs perfectly in this life? Hence the reborn use their freedom of will in this life both to do well and to do badly.

So there can be no question whether a man, given the help of grace, truly has free choice' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 13). The same author repeats this in chapter 28 of that book: 'In the state of grace the renewed will chooses good freely, in such a way that while it is effectively moved by grace to choose it, it can indeed choose the opposite through the defect of nature, but does not will to, because of the efficacy of grace.'
